title: Two weaknesses: press, switch or keep the siege
outcomes: In an unlabeled position decides between pressing the weakness he already attacks and switching to a second one, and prefers the move that keeps the first attack alive
Tests the second-target move against the engine instead of assuming that a new target is progress
Says when no weak pawn exists, so there is nothing to switch to

steps.text: In *Two weaknesses: add a second target* you found a move that adds a second weak pawn to your attack. Now you **choose**: keep pressing the first weakness, or switch to a second one. The aim is to keep the first attack alive so the opponent cannot fix it while the new target appears. Rule of thumb: a move that keeps the old attack and adds a new one is a candidate; test it, because a new target is not progress by itself.

steps.caption: Black to move. Black already attacks the isolated pawn on f3. White's h-pawns are weak too. Which move keeps the first attack and adds another?

line.say: Qf4 keeps the attack on f3 and adds one on h2.

claims.statement: The white pawns on f3 and h2 are isolated.
After Qf4, Black attacks f3 once.
After Qf4, Black attacks h2 once.
At depth 16 Qf4 is the engine's best move.

steps.text: **Conditions.** Switching works when the new attack keeps the old one and costs nothing elsewhere. It fails when the move that adds the target gives something up, and it does not apply when the opponent has no weak pawn. Rule of thumb: if the opponent can fix the first weakness, look for a second one he cannot fix at the same time. Compare the two positions below.

steps.title: Two positions, two verdicts
steps.prompt: Two unrelated positions. In each a move adds a second attack while the first stays. Find the engine's choice, then see whether the second-target move was it.
Think about the positions you played without hints. Write one line each.
